newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish troops launch anti-rebel drive into Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish troops launch anti-rebel drive into Iraq.

text.p: Heavily-armed Turkish troops have poured into northern Iraq in their latest bid to crush a persistent separatist insurgency by guerrillas of the Kurdistan Workers Party.

Thousands of troops, backed by tanks, artillery and air power, moved in before dawn on Wednesday and drove rebel PKK units toward Iraqi government lines well to the south, reports from the remote region said.
Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said the operation was a "humanitarian mission" to protect Iraqi Kurds from the PKK.
"The troops will withdraw when the operation is over," he told reporters. Turkish army officers in Iraq were tight-lipped.
Baghdad demanded an immediate withdrawal, saying the incursion breached international law. It said there were many casualties.

The Turkish assault followed a security sweep by local Kurdish authorities, who ordered all journalists to leave the area around Zakho, the main Iraqi border town. The border was sealed to civilian traffic.

A Western photographer who provides pictures for Reuters said his film was confiscated and he was expelled from Zakho shortly before the operation began. Local officials told him they had been ordered to impose a "news blackout".
"Around 10,000 troops have crossed over from around Habur," said a Turkish official near the Habur border crossing.
Residents said the troops were supported by up to 100 tanks and armoured personnel carriers. U.S.-made Cobra helicopters provided air support, they said.

The anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Concress, citing what it said were satellite telephone contacts inside Iraq, said Turkish forces had cut the road between Dohuk, one of the main cities of the Kurdish north, and the Baghdad-controlled city of Mosul.

PKK fighters had fallen back under the assault, with some forced to flee the "safe haven," carved out by Western forces to protect the Kurds after the Gulf war, for the safety of government territory. Others moved east toward Iran.

With reporters barred from the immediate area by gunmen of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) -- the region's leading Iraqi Kurdish faction and a strong PKK rival -- it was impossible to confirm the scope of the Turkish thrust.
A Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman said the operation was a "limited" one, at the invitation of the Iraqi Kurds, to expel PKK guerrillas from bases along the border.
However, a senior security source told Reuters: "This is a wide and comprehensive operation."
Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency reported clashes between troops and the PKK in a region it called Sarisarilar. It said troops backed by helicopters had inflicted heavy losses on the rebels.

The assault followed weeks of steady build-up by Turkish forces, who have been unable to eradicte the PKK in more than 12 years of fighting that has claimed around 22,000 lives. Clashes inside Turkey had also intensified in recent days.

"In the last month there have been coachloads of soldiers brought through the town, dozens of coaches at a time," one man told Reuters correspondent Daren Butler in the Turkish town of Cizre, 45 km (30 miles) from the border.
Police prevented reporters from moving beyond Cizre and trying to cross the border.
A line of lorries, about seven km (four miles) long formed otuside the town as drivers waited for the border to reopen to their illict -- but tolerated -- trade in smuggled Iraqi oil.
The Iraqi side of the border is under the general control of Massoud Barzani's KDP. Iraqi opposition sources said the KDP had been fighting the PKK since Monday.
Northern Iraq was set up as a Western-backed autonomous Kurdish area following the 1991 Gulf War. The KDP and another Kurdish group have shared power, if acrimoniously, since then.
Barzani teamed up last year with forces of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein against rival Iraqi Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani, prompting U.S. missile strikes against Iraqi targets.

Turkish troops regularly cross back and forth in "hot pursuit" of the PKK. In March 1995, tens of thousands pushed deep into Iraq for a prolonged campaign that drove the PKK back but failed to fulfill their stated goal of ending the insurgency.
